cues.text: A Church Divided by Schism
The death of Pope Honorius II in 1130 triggered a disputed election that split the College of Cardinals.
One faction elected Innocent II ; another elected the wealthy Roman noble Anacletus II , born Pietro Pierleoni into one of Rome's most powerful banking families.
Anacletus controlled Rome itself, backed by the Pierleoni family's immense wealth and, crucially, by Roger II of Sicily , whom he rewarded with a royal crown in exchange for military support.
Innocent II was forced into exile, first to France and then across much of Western Europe seeking recognition.
Innocent found his strongest advocate in St. Bernard of Clairvaux , the most influential churchman of his generation.
Bernard’s tireless preaching and diplomacy across France, England, and Germany rallied Western Christendom’s great powers behind Innocent’s claim as the legitimate pope.
The support of Emperor Lothair II proved decisive, and by degrees Anacletus's support crumbled, leaving him an isolated figure controlling little beyond the city of Rome itself.
The Schism Ends

The schism resolved itself not through a council but through death: Anacletus died in January 1138, and his short-lived successor soon submitted to Innocent, ending nearly eight years of division at the very top of the Church's hierarchy.
To repair the damage, Innocent II sought to depose clergy improperly ordained by the antipope's faction and condemn errors that had spread amid the disorder.
He also sought to reform abuses among clergy and laity alike, convoking a general council at the Lateran for April 1139.
Nearly a thousand prelates from across Western Christendom attended, an assembly even larger than the First Lateran Council sixteen years earlier.
Innocent presided in person and opened proceedings by formally deposing all those ordained by Anacletus and his chief partisans.
Condemning New Errors
Beyond settling the schism, the council turned to doctrinal errors that had begun circulating in these same years.
It condemned the followers of Peter of Bruys and Henry of Lausanne , itinerant preachers who rejected infant baptism, the Eucharist, and clerical authority.
It also censured the reforming zeal of Arnold of Brescia , a former student of Peter Abelard who argued the clergy should renounce property and temporal power altogether.
Roger II of Sicily , who had persisted in supporting Anacletus's cause even after the antipope's death, was excommunicated by the council for his continued defiance.
Disciplinary Reforms

Among its thirty canons, the council reaffirmed and sharpened earlier prohibitions on clerical marriage, declaring invalid any marriage contracted by those in major orders, monks, or professed religious — a stricter standard than some earlier councils had enforced.
It also renewed condemnations of simony and usury, echoing a growing concern of the age with contemporary warfare’s brutality.
It forbade using crossbows and siege engines against Christians, a rare early attempt at limiting the weapons of war.
The council thereby combined institutional housekeeping — cleaning up the wreckage of a papal schism — with a broader ambition to reform clerical discipline and public morals across the Latin Church.
Legacy

Second Lateran closed one of the most disruptive papal schisms of the twelfth century and reaffirmed, with unusual severity, the Church's expectations of clerical celibacy — a standard that has remained normative for the Latin Church's secular clergy ever since.
Its condemnation of Arnold of Brescia proved only a temporary setback for him.
He would go on to lead a populist uprising in Rome itself in the 1140s before his eventual execution in 1155.
This reminds us that conciliar condemnation did not always translate into the swift silencing of a determined critic.
